sentences.text: Vegavis lived in Antarctica during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 65 million years ago.
The genus existed from 72.2 to 66 million years ago throughout the Maastrichtian period.
It is classified within the order Anseriformes and the family Vegaviidae.
The discovery of Vegavis iaai demonstrates that major groups of living birds had already diversified by the Cretaceous.
Its syrinx possessed an asymmetrical third segment and large soft-tissue resonating structures, suggesting it could produce honks like ducks and geese.

The type species Vegavis iaai was named in 2005 based on fossils from the López de Bertodano Formation, though the specimen was found in 1992 and described later due to its delicate nature embedded in a concretion.

The holotype specimen, which is the specimen the species is based on, is held by the Museo de La Plata in Argentina and was studied using CT scans to examine bone structure without damaging the fossil.
A nearly complete skull discovered in 2011 was officially described in 2025 and assigned to Vegavis.

Two additional species, Vegavis geitononesos and Vegavis notopothousa, were named in 2026 based on material from the López de Bertodano Formation, with the type locality for V. geitononesos dating to the uppermost Maastrichtian.
Vegavis had a high metabolism that allowed it to survive at high latitudes in Antarctica.
The bird exhibited osteosclerosis, a condition possibly related to variations in diving behavior.
Some paleontologists debate whether Vegavis belongs to Anseriformes or is a stem-group bird with an unresolved position at the base of Neognathae.
